the synovium from hemophilic subjects is highly angiogenic and that angiogenic factors are increased in the peripheral blood of these subjects.

the identification of the pathogenic mechanisms involved in the development of hemophilia-related synovitis.

the development and progression of hemarthrosis in patients with hemophilia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hemophilic synoviopathy is characterized by neoangiogenesis, and that VEGF-A is a key player in this process.

hemophilic synoviocytes and macrophages, as well as endothelial progenitor and hematopoietic cells in peripheral blood, may play a critical role in the neoangiogenic response in hemophilia, which is mediated by VEGF and other proangiogenic factors.
hemophilic synoviocytes and monocytes/macrophages secrete proangiogenic cytokines and growth factors that induce neoangiogenesis and synovitis in hemophilic joints.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the angiogenic response observed in HJD subjects could be a potential target for therapeutic interventions.
the neoangiogenesis in HJD may be mediated by VEGF-A and that VEGFR2 may be an important target for the prevention of hemophilic arthropathy.
the neoangiogenesis in the synovial tissue of HJD subjects is mediated by a complex interaction of angiogenic factors and proinflammatory cells, which may contribute to the pathogenesis of HJD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hemophilic synovitits is a chronic inflammatory condition that is associated with neoangiogenesis.
neoangiogenesis is an early and critical event in the pathogenesis and progression of hemarthrotic joint disease.
the angiogenic response in HJD may be mediated via VEGF and that VEGF inhibition could be a novel approach for the management of HJD.
